content: Now the serpent was more subtle than any animal of the field which the LORD God had made. He said to the woman, “Has God really said, ‘You shall not eat of any tree of the garden’?” {{v:2}} The woman said to the serpent, “We may eat fruit from the trees of the garden, {{v:3}} but not the fruit of the tree which is in the middle of the garden. God has said, ‘You shall not eat of it. You shall not touch it, lest you die.’” {{v:4}} The serpent said to the woman, “You won’t really die, {{v:5}} for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” {{v:6}} When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate. Then she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too. {{v:7}} Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves. {{v:8}} They heard the LORD God’s voice walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of the LORD God among the trees of the garden. {{v:9}} The LORD God called to the man, and said to him, “Where are you?” {{v:10}} The man said, “I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; so I hid myself.” {{v:11}} God said, “Who told you that you were naked? Have you eaten from the tree that I commanded you not to eat from?” {{v:12}} The man said, “The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.” {{v:13}} The LORD God said to the woman, “What have you done?” The woman said, “The serpent deceived me, and I ate.” {{v:14}} The LORD God said to the serpent, “Because you have done this, you are cursed above all livestock, and above every animal of the field. You shall go on your belly and you shall eat dust all the days of your life. {{v:15}} I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.” {{v:16}} To the woman he said, “I will greatly multiply your pain in childbirth. You will bear children in pain. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.” {{v:17}} To Adam he said, “Because you have listened to your wife’s voice, and have eaten from the tree, about which I commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat of it,’ the ground is cursed for your sake. You will eat from it with much labor all the days of your life. {{v:18}} It will yield thorns and thistles to you; and you will eat the herb of the field. {{v:19}} You will eat bread by the sweat of your face until you return to the ground, for you were taken out of it. For you are dust, and you shall return to dust.” {{v:20}} The man called his wife Eve because she would be the mother of all the living. {{v:21}} The LORD God made garments of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them. {{v:22}} The LORD God said, “Behold, the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. Now, lest he reach out his hand, and also take of the tree of life, and eat, and live forever—” {{v:23}} Therefore the LORD God sent him out from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from which he was taken. {{v:24}} So he drove out the man; and he placed cherubim at the east of the garden of Eden, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to guard the way to the tree of life.

facets.text: The serpent's opening move is to distort God's word, exaggerating the prohibition into "any tree of the garden," and then flatly contradicting the warning of death with "You won't really die." Temptation works by casting doubt on God's goodness and truthfulness, insinuating that God withholds the good out of jealousy rather than love. The lie that eating will make them "like God, knowing good and evil" reframes trusting obedience as servitude and rebellion as self-fulfillment.
facets.question: How does temptation distort the truth about God's goodness?

facets.text: The threefold appeal—the tree was "good for food," "a delight to the eyes," and "to be desired to make one wise"—maps the anatomy of sin as disordered desire seizing what God has not given. The tradition sees here the pattern later named as concupiscence of the flesh, of the eyes, and the pride of life. Sin begins not merely in an act but in a will that prefers a created good to the Creator and grasps at autonomy from Him.
facets.question: What is the inner structure of temptation and sin?

facets.text: Original sin is a shared act: the woman is deceived and eats, then gives to her husband "with her," and he eats too. Adam, given the command directly and standing beside her, fails to guard and correct, so that Scripture and tradition lay the decisive responsibility on him as head. The Fall thereby fractures the communion of the first couple and infects the whole human family they represent.
facets.question: How were both Adam and Eve responsible for the first sin?

facets.text: The immediate fruit of sin is not the promised divinity but shame, fear, hiding, and mutual accusation. Their eyes are opened only to their own nakedness; they cover themselves and flee the God who once walked with them in the cool of the day. Sin ruptures the harmony of body and soul, of person with God, and of person with person, as Adam blames the woman and even God who gave her.
facets.question: What are the real consequences of sin on human relationships and interior peace?

facets.text: God's question "Where are you?" is not ignorance but a merciful summons, calling the hiding sinner out of concealment into the light of confession. Even in judgment God seeks the man first, drawing out his admission before pronouncing sentence. This searching call anticipates the whole economy of grace in which God takes the initiative to recover the lost.
facets.question: Why does God call out to Adam instead of simply condemning him?

facets.text: In cursing the serpent God promises hostility between the serpent and the woman, and between their offspring, foretelling that her seed "will bruise your head." The Catholic tradition reads this Protoevangelium as the first announcement of the Gospel, fulfilled in Christ the promised Seed who crushes Satan, and associates the victorious Woman with Mary the New Eve. Judgment itself becomes the vessel of the first promise of redemption.
facets.question: What is the Protoevangelium and how does it point to Christ and Mary?

facets.text: The sentences on the woman and the man—pain in childbearing, disordered relations between spouses, and toil against a cursed ground yielding thorns—are not arbitrary punishments but the unfolding of sin's inherent damage to the goods of marriage, family, and work. Death enters as the return of dust to dust, the wage of separation from God. These consequences describe the wounded condition of human life outside Eden that redemption must heal.
facets.question: Why does the Fall bring suffering, toil, and death into human life?

facets.text: God clothes Adam and Eve with garments of animal skins, an act of tender provision that requires the death of a creature to cover human shame. The tradition sees here a foreshadowing of the covering of sin through sacrifice, ultimately the sacrifice of Christ who clothes the redeemed in grace. Even as He passes sentence, God cares for the bodily and spiritual dignity of the fallen.
facets.question: What is the meaning of God clothing Adam and Eve with animal skins?

facets.text: Expulsion from the garden and the cherubim guarding the tree of life are an act of mercy as well as judgment: God prevents humanity from eating the tree of life and living forever in a fallen, unredeemed state. Death becomes a boundary against the perpetuation of misery, and the guarded way to life awaits reopening. Christ, the new and living way, restores access to the tree of life, imaged in the Cross and the Eucharist.
facets.question: Why did God bar Adam and Eve from the tree of life, and how is that access restored?

facets.text: Adam names his wife Eve, "the mother of all the living," at the very moment of judgment and mortality. This act of naming, spoken in hope after the promise of the crushing Seed, is an affirmation of faith that life and future generations will continue despite the sentence of death. Human hope survives the Fall because God's promise has already been given.
facets.question: Why does Adam name his wife 'mother of all the living' right after the Fall?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: Genesis 3 narrates the Fall—the serpent's temptation, the first sin, God's merciful judgment, and expulsion from Eden—establishing original sin, its consequences, and the first promise of redemption. Doctrinal scope covers original sin, concupiscence, the Protoevangelium, Mary as New Eve, and Christ the promised Seed.

[MORAL | traditional]: Temptation works by distorting God's word and casting doubt on His goodness, reframing obedience as servitude and rebellion as becoming "like God."
[MORAL | traditional]: The threefold appeal (good for food, delight to eyes, desirable for wisdom) reveals sin as disordered desire and concupiscence preferring created goods to the Creator.
[DOCTRINAL | traditional]: Original sin is a shared act of the first couple, with decisive responsibility on Adam as head, fracturing the communion of humanity they represent.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: Sin's true fruit is shame, fear, hiding, and mutual accusation, rupturing harmony with God, self, and neighbor.
[DEVOTIONAL | inferential]: God's "Where are you?" is a merciful summons drawing the sinner from hiding to confession, prefiguring the economy of grace.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: The Protoevangelium promises the woman's Seed who crushes the serpent's head, fulfilled in Christ and associated with Mary the New Eve.
[DOCTRINAL | explicit]: The sentences of pain, disordered spousal relations, toil, and death describe sin's inherent damage to marriage, family, work, and the wage of separation from God.
[TYPOLOGICAL | inferential]: God's clothing of Adam and Eve in animal skins foreshadows the covering of sin through sacrifice, ultimately Christ's.
[TYPOLOGICAL | traditional]: Barring the tree of life is mercy preventing eternal fallen misery; Christ reopens the guarded way to life in Cross and Eucharist.
[DEVOTIONAL | inferential]: Adam naming Eve "mother of all the living" is an act of faith and hope grounded in God's promise of the crushing Seed.
